title: Heritage sites in Chhattisgarh: Sirpur, Tala and Bastar
seo_title: Heritage Sites in Chhattisgarh: Temples and History Guide
meta_description: Heritage sites in Chhattisgarh, from Sirpur's brick temple and Tala's sculpture to Bhoramdeo, Ramgarh's caves and Bastar's living traditions, with museums.
summary: Chhattisgarh's heritage centres on early brick and stone temples at Sirpur, Tala, Malhar, Rajim and Kharod, the 11th-century Bhoramdeo temple, the Ramgarh caves with early inscriptions, rock art at Singhanpur, and the living traditions of Bastar. The state has no UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sections.h2: Why Chhattisgarh matters for Indian heritage
paras: Ancient Dakshina Kosala, roughly the Mahanadi basin of today's Chhattisgarh, was ruled from about the 5th to 8th centuries by the Sharabhapuriya and Panduvamshi dynasties, later by Kalachuri branches based at Ratanpur, by the Phani Nagavanshis in Kawardha, and by the Nagas and Kakatiya-descended rulers in Bastar. Many of its temples are early, and some of the best examples of brick temple building in India survive here.

The state is also home to a large Adivasi population, and much of its heritage is living: Gond, Muria, Maria, Halba and other communities keep traditions in metalwork, wood, festivals and village shrines. Their traditions are as much a part of the state's heritage as its temples.

Sirpur, on the Mahanadi, was the Panduvamshi capital Shripura. Its Lakshmana temple, of the 7th century, is one of the finest brick temples in India, with carved brick on its tower and a stone doorframe. Excavations from the 2000s exposed Buddhist monasteries, a market area and the large Surang Tila temple platform. Sirpur shows Shaiva, Vaishnava, Buddhist and Jain buildings in one town.

Malhar, near Bilaspur, has a long sequence from early historic layers to medieval temples such as the Pataleshwar and Deur temples. Tala has the Devrani and Jethani temples, usually dated to around the 5th to 6th centuries, and a famous standing figure built up of animal forms, often identified as a form of Rudra Shiva. Our session on [early structural temples](early-structural-temples.html) puts Tala and Sirpur in context.

At Ramgarh hill in Surguja, the Sitabenga and Jogimara caves carry early Brahmi inscriptions, and Sitabenga is sometimes described as an early theatre because of its seating arrangement; scholars debate that reading. Rock shelters with paintings are found at Singhanpur and Kabra Pahad, in Raigarh district.

The Rajiv Lochan temple at Rajim, at the meeting of the Mahanadi, Pairi and Sondur rivers, is an early Vishnu temple with carved pillars, and the area holds a large annual fair. The Lakshmaneshwar temple at Kharod and the Shiva temple at Pali are other early examples. The Vishnu temple at Janjgir was left incomplete.

Bhoramdeo, near Kawardha, is an 11th-century Nagara temple of the Phani Nagavanshi rulers, sometimes called the Khajuraho of Chhattisgarh for its sculpture, though it is smaller. The Bhand Deval at Arang is a Jain temple. In Bastar, Barsur has temples of the Naga period, and the Danteshwari temple at Dantewada remains central to the Bastar Dussehra festival. Our [Nagara temple architecture](nagara-temple-architecture.html) session explains how to read these towers.

Bastar Dussehra is one of India's longest festivals, running for about 75 days, and centres on the goddess Danteshwari and the participation of village communities rather than the story of Rama. Dhokra metal casting by the lost-wax method, wrought iron work and wood carving are practised by local artisans, and weekly haats are important social spaces.

Visitors should treat village shrines, ghotul traditions and festivals as community life, not spectacle. Our programme on [community archaeology and heritage stewardship](community-archaeology-and-heritage-stewardship.html) discusses how to do that well.

sections.h2: How to read a Chhattisgarh temple
paras: Many of the state's early temples survive only in part, so it helps to know what to look for. At Sirpur, Rajim and Kharod, start at the doorframe: early doorways carry river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna at the base, bands of creepers and couples, and a figure on the lintel that tells you which deity the temple was built for. Then look at the plan, which is often a square sanctum with a small hall, and at the tower, if it survives, to see whether it is built in courses of brick or stone.

At Tala the temples are ruined to their lower walls, and the sculpture is the main evidence. At Bhoramdeo the tower is complete and the outer walls are crowded with carved figures, which makes it a good place to compare an 11th-century Nagara temple with the much earlier ones nearby. Groups that want to practise recording what they see can add our [temple architectural documentation lab](temple-architectural-documentation-lab.html), which teaches measured sketching and photography for temples.

Inscriptions matter here too. Copper plates and stone inscriptions of the Sharabhapuriya and Panduvamshi kings name donors, villages and officials, and they are the main source for the region's early history. The script is a regional development of Brahmi with box-headed letters, which is a good subject for a lesson on [India's scripts from Brahmi to Sarada](reading-india-s-scripts-brahmi-to-sarada.html).

sections.h2: Does Chhattisgarh have a UNESCO site?
paras: No. Chhattisgarh has no inscribed World Heritage Site as of October 2026. Its early temples are protected nationally, but none is on the World Heritage List.

sections.h2: Planning a heritage trip in Chhattisgarh
paras: Raipur is the base for Sirpur, Rajim and Arang; Bilaspur for Tala, Malhar, Ratanpur and Kharod; Kawardha for Bhoramdeo; Jagdalpur for Bastar. Distances are moderate and roads are generally good. Check the state archaeology department or ASI website before you go.
Chhattisgarh visits are planned around each group. We design [a study tour for your group](a-study-tour-built-for-your-group.html), and families can ask about [private journeys](journeys.html).

faq.q: What are the main historical places in Chhattisgarh?
faq.a: Sirpur, Tala, Malhar, Rajim, Bhoramdeo, Kharod, Ratanpur, the Ramgarh caves and the Singhanpur rock shelters are the main ones, with Barsur and Dantewada in Bastar for later temples and living traditions.

faq.q: Is there any UNESCO World Heritage Site in Chhattisgarh?
faq.a: No. Chhattisgarh has no inscribed World Heritage Site as of October 2026. Its early temples at Sirpur and Tala are nationally important and protected, but they are not on the World Heritage List.

faq.q: Why is the Lakshmana temple at Sirpur famous?
faq.a: It is one of the best preserved brick temples in India, built around the 7th century, with carved brick on its tower and a finely worked stone doorframe. It shows how brick temples looked before stone became the norm.

faq.q: Can Talaash Heritage organise a study tour to Chhattisgarh?
faq.a: Yes, on request. We design custom study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, for example Sirpur, Rajim, Tala and Malhar, with a lecture on temple architecture or rock art beforehand.

posts.hook: One of India's finest temples is made of brick.
posts.caption: The Lakshmana temple at Sirpur, of about the 7th century, has carved brick on its tower and a stone doorframe. It survived where many brick temples did not.

posts.hook: At Tala, look closely at the standing figure.
posts.caption: The famous sculpture at Tala is built up from animal forms: lizards, fish, peacocks and lions. Count how many you can find before reading the label.
